title: Mood's Median Test
factorSelcted: Select the factor variable (groups to compare)
confLevel: Confidence level for the median confidence intervals (between 0 and 1, default 0.95)

help.title: Mood's Median Test Pro
help.body:
Description
Mood's median test is a nonparametric test of whether two or more independent groups have the same population median.

How it works
1. The overall (grand) median of all the observations is computed.
2. For each group, the observations at or below the overall median (N<=) and above it (N>) are counted.
3. A Pearson chi-square test of association is run on the resulting groups x 2 table. DF = number of groups - 1.

The null hypothesis is that all population medians are equal. The alternative hypothesis is that not all population medians are equal. If the p-value is less than or equal to your significance level (for example 0.05), at least one group median differs.

Output
Descriptive statistics - for each group and for all data combined: N, median, N<=, N>, the interquartile range (Q3 - Q1) and a confidence interval for the median. The confidence interval is the nonlinear interpolation interval from the one-sample sign test. For a group with fewer than six observations the achieved confidence level is lower than the requested level (reported in the table footer).
Test - DF, chi-square statistic and p-value.
Boxplot (optional) - one box per group with a dashed line at the overall median. The box edges are Q1 and Q3 and the line inside the box is the group median, computed the same way as in the descriptive table. Whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 x (Q3 - Q1) of the box and points beyond are shown as circles. The option to print the median, Q1 and Q3 values next to each box applies when the boxplot is shown.

Notes
Only groups with two or more observations are included in the analysis. Rows with a missing response or group are dropped.
If the selected grouping variable is not already a factor (for example text, numeric or logical), it is converted to a factor internally for the analysis. The dataset itself is not changed, and a note is added to the output.
The test assumes the groups have similar shape and spread. Check the Q3 - Q1 column and the boxplot; very different values suggest this assumption may not hold.
If no observation is above the overall median (many ties at the median), values equal to the overall median are counted as above the median so the test can be computed. A note is added to the output when this happens.
The chi-square approximation is less reliable when expected counts are small (less than 5). A note is added to the output when this happens.
Mood's median test is less powerful than the Kruskal-Wallis test when the data are not heavily affected by outliers.
